description: Faculty team from Jyothi Engineering College (Autonomous), Thrissur, Kerala, India, with Electronics, Computer Science and Mechatronics backgrounds. We teach, mentor student innovators and build projects in embedded systems, IoT, robotics, solar energy and software. Our project, Outpost 30 (https://jecstars.earth), is a free browser game where kids aged 7-12 run a Moon or Mars outpost using real NASA data. Strengths: hardware, coding, web, data and school outreach.
summary: Outpost 30 is a free browser game that puts children aged 7–12 in charge of a Moon or Mars outpost for 30 days. Every day, players share a limited supply of solar power between life support, food, radiation shielding and science. No choice is free: power spent on science today can leave the crew short of air during a dark spell, and skipping shields can push radiation over the limit when a solar storm hits. Every event is grounded in real data: archived solar flares from NASA's Space Weather Database (DONKI), surface radiation rates measured on the Moon and on Mars, NASA's astronaut radiation limits (NASA-STD-3001), and spaceflight health findings from NASA's Open Science Data Repository (OSDR). Children leave having experienced, not just read about, the trade-offs that NASA mission planners face every day.
details:
1. What Outpost 30 does

•     Runs a 30-day mission at one of two real sites: near the Moon's south pole (the region planned for NASA's Artemis missions) or in Jezero Crater on Mars (where NASA's Perseverance rover works).

•     Gives a daily power budget from solar panels. Players split it between Air, Greenhouse, Shield and Science. Unused power is stored in a battery with a fixed size.

•     Throws real-world events at the crew: solar storms based on real NASA-recorded flares, dark spells, dust storms, air leaks, damaged panels, mould in the greenhouse and exercise needs. Each event has two or three choices, and every choice has a cost.

•     Shows the consequences before they happen. Each bar previews tomorrow's value, so children can test “what if” before pressing End Day.

•     Ends with a learning debrief: stars, a day-by-day chart of air, food and radiation, and “What you learned” points based on what happened in that game.

•     Tells kids where the science comes from. A “Show me the science” view shows the real numbers, and a “Data sources” page lists every dataset with links.

2. How it works: the trade-off engine

We used only three survival needs plus one goal, as the challenge brief recommends. All rules are simple whole numbers, so a child can do the arithmetic in their head.

Figure 1. A solar storm based on the real X7.1 flare of 1 October 2024. Each choice shows its radiation cost before the player decides.

3. Two worlds, two different lessons

Figure 2. Mars dust storm event, based on the 2018 storm that ended NASA's Opportunity rover.

4. Real NASA data inside the game

 

Live data: the “📡 Live space weather” button calls the NASA DONKI flare web service (ccmc.gsfc.nasa.gov/DONKI-API, its current address since late 2026, with the older api.nasa.gov address as a backup) for the last 30 days and can put those live flares into the next game. When live data is not reachable, the game says so clearly and uses the archived flares. Stored data is never shown as live.

Figure 3. “Show me the science” view: each bar explains the real number behind it and its source.

5. Evidence: does the game really teach the trade-off?

We tested the balance with 1,200 automated games (200 per strategy per site), comparing three player styles:

•     Careful plan: feed air and food, build 3 shield layers early, save battery before dark spells, and use the rest for science.

•     All science, no safety: minimum air and food, no shields, and keep working through solar storms.

•     Random clicks: no planning at all.

Figure 4. Mission outcomes from 1,200 test games.

Figure 5. Average crew radiation dose by strategy. The dashed line is the game's mission limit.

What this shows:

•     Careful planning survived every test game on both worlds, with an average Moon dose of about 39 mSv.

•     Ignoring safety on the Moon failed in every test game, 94% of them from radiation (average dose about 100 mSv, over the 75 mSv limit). The game rewards planning, not luck.

•     On Mars, the same risky plan survived 73% of the time. This matches the real science: Mars's atmosphere gives some protection, so there the hard part is power, not radiation.

•     Random play almost always ran out of air, which shows the core life-support lesson.

6. Designed for ages 7–12

•     Plain words: terms like mSv, sol and regolith are explained when they first appear.

•     Big buttons, emoji labels, and a robot helper (Rovy) who gives one tip at a time.

•     Failure is a lesson: a mission that ends early shows a friendly tip for next time.

•     Replayable: events, storm days and dark-spell timing change every game.

•     Sound effects for each event, with a mute button.

•     Works on phones, tablets and laptops in any browser, with no login or download.

•     For teachers and parents: learning goals, discussion questions and a classroom activity are built in.

Figure 6. Phone layout

7. Testing with children

✏️ Add notes from real children playing: age range, what confused them, what they enjoyed, and what you changed. Space Apps rule: do NOT include any child's name, photo, voice or likeness.

8. What we simplified (and why)

•     Time: dark spells are shortened (a real lunar night away from the poles lasts about 14 Earth days).

•     Solar storm dose: estimated from flare size (about 5 mSv per X-class unit, unshielded, on the Moon). Real storms vary widely, so this is labelled “game estimate” in the game.

•     Units: air, food and power use simple units instead of kg or kWh, so children can calculate them.

•     Shields: layers stand for regolith and water walls. Their stronger effect on solar particles than on cosmic rays follows real physics.

10. Roadmap

•     Hands-on control panel: an Arduino box with 3 slide controls for the power split and LEDs for storm alerts, linked to the browser by Web Serial.

•     Live RadLab data: show a real ISS dose reading for today next to the game's dose.

•     Classroom mode: several teams run bases and compare results on one screen.

•     More languages: Malayalam, Hindi and others.

•     Real Mars Trek terrain as the background for the Mars base.

Play the game: https://jecstars.earth/

Free, browser-based, no login or download. Works on phones, tablets and laptops. Hosted on our own domain, jecstars.earth, using GoDaddy free hosting from the NASA Space Apps Global Offers.
